outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the lower bound on the minimum area of a convex universal cover has risen twice, from 0.832 to 0.833 (Xie, June 2026) and to 0.8344 (Mishra, August 2026, computer-assisted), with a 0.834 bound (Zeng, September 2026) posted a day after Mishra's; the upper bound 0.8440935944 (Gibbs, 2018 preprint) is unchanged, and the minimising shape and its exact area remain unknown.
problem_asks: (1) Identify the convex planar set of least area that contains a congruent copy (under translation, rotation and reflection, per the Wikipedia wording) of every planar set of diameter one. (2) Determine that least area, i.e. the infimum of areas of convex universal covers; the statement presupposes it is attained (existence by compactness, as a secondary report of Baez's 2015 blog post notes). Convexity is a stated restriction: non-convex covers (Duff 1980) answer a different question. The statement asks for the shape and the value, not for bounds on the value.

events.what_happened: Gyula Pál, 'Ueber ein elementares Variationsproblem', Danske Mat.-Fys. Meddelelser III 2 (1920), 1-35. Lebesgue posed the problem to Pál in a 1914 letter (Wikipedia). Pál showed that a regular hexagon with inscribed circle of diameter 1 is a universal cover (area √3/2 ≈ 0.8660), that a cover for all curves of constant width one also covers all sets of diameter one, and that removing two corners of the hexagon gives a universal cover of area 2 − 2/√3 ≈ 0.84530.
events.delivers: Upper bound 2 − 2/√3 ≈ 0.84530 on the minimum area of a convex universal cover (the hexagon itself gives √3/2 ≈ 0.8660). Also reduces covering all diameter-one sets to covering curves of constant width one.
events.remains: Parts (1) and (2) of problem_asks: the minimising shape and its exact area are not determined; this is only an upper bound.

checked_by.who: Ujjwal Mishra (author of the 2026 preprint arXiv:2608.30538)
checked_by.qualification: Active researcher on the problem; his own computation
checked_by.what_they_did: Reports reproducing Pál's constant in the author's own code, according to the paper's text (fetched HTML, v2)

events.directly_checkable: The hexagon and two-corner-removed cover can be checked by hand from the explicit geometry; the 2015 authors cite a Java program and a Mathematica notebook by Greg Egan for the corner-removal areas (referenced in the 2015 paper; not opened).
events.direction: Upper bound: cuts the minimum downward from the hexagon's 0.8660 to 0.84530.
events.object: Explicit covers: the regular hexagon with inscribed circle of diameter 1 (area √3/2), and that hexagon with two corners removed, area 2 − 2/√3 ≈ 0.84529946 (Wikipedia, Pál 1920). The covering proof is analytic.

events.what_happened: Roland Sprague, 'Über ein elementares Variationsproblem', Matematiska Tidsskrift Ser. B (1936), 96-99. Removes a further piece from another corner of Pál's cover and keeps it a cover; the resulting bound a ≤ 0.844137708436 is quoted by Baez, Bagdasaryan and Gibbs (2015). The original paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Upper bound 0.844137708436 on the minimum convex cover area, from Pál's cover with one further corner piece removed.
events.remains: Minimising shape and exact area (parts (1) and (2) of problem_asks).
events.directly_checkable: The removed piece is a corner region of Pál's cover; checkable by hand from the geometry (not checked here).
events.direction: Upper bound: cuts the minimum downward further.
events.object: Explicit covering set: Pál's cover with a corner piece removed; area ≤ 0.844137708436 as quoted by Baez, Bagdasaryan and Gibbs (2015). The removed piece is described in a search summary as bounded by two circular arcs; not verified against the original.

events.what_happened: G. F. D. Duff, 'A smaller universal cover for sets of unit diameter', C. R. Math. Acad. Sci. 2 (1980), 37-42. Drops the convexity requirement and obtains a non-convex universal cover of smaller area than the convex covers then known (per Baez, Bagdasaryan and Gibbs 2015). The paper was not opened; its area value was not found.
events.delivers: A non-convex universal cover of smaller area than the convex covers then known. Different question: the problem restricts to convex covers, so this does not bear on the convex minimum.
events.remains: All of problem_asks; the convex minimum is unaffected.
events.direction: Different question (convexity dropped). Cuts neither way on the convex minimum.
events.object: A non-convex universal cover of smaller area than the convex covers then known. The set and its area were not read.

events.what_happened: H. C. Hansen, 'Small universal covers for sets of unit diameter', Geom. Ded. 42 (1992), 205-213. Removes two further small pieces from the Pál–Sprague shape. Baez, Bagdasaryan and Gibbs (2015) show that Hansen's last removal was 8·10⁻²¹ in area, not the 6·10⁻¹⁸ he claimed. Secondary sources say Hansen's reductions ran from 1975 to 1992; the earlier work was not located, so the year given is 1992.
events.delivers: Upper bound: a further reduction of the Pál–Sprague cover. Its last step removes 8·10⁻²¹ in area (per the 2015 correction), not the 6·10⁻¹⁸ claimed. Restricted to the convex Pál family.
events.remains: Minimising shape and exact area (parts (1) and (2)).

checked_by.who: John Baez, Karine Bagdasaryan, Philip Gibbs (authors of the 2015 paper)
checked_by.qualification: Researchers who re-ran the corner-removal areas numerically with a Java program and a Mathematica notebook by Greg Egan; Quanta (2018) describes Gibbs as an amateur, not a professional mathematician
checked_by.what_they_did: Re-checked Hansen's last reduction and found the removed area was 8·10⁻²¹, not 6·10⁻¹⁸; published in J. Comput. Geom. 6(1) (2015) 288-299

events.directly_checkable: The size of the last removal is a small area computation; the 2015 paper gives the corrected figure and cites the programs used (not opened).
events.doubts: Hansen's stated area for his last removal (6·10⁻¹⁸) was wrong by a factor of about 750 according to the 2015 authors. The correction concerns the size of the claimed reduction; the 2015 paper continues to use the Pál–Sprague–Hansen cover as its starting shape.
events.direction: Upper bound: cuts the minimum downward, by far less than Hansen claimed.
events.object: Explicit covering set: the Pál–Sprague cover with two further small slivers removed (each bounded by two straight lines and an arc, per a search summary; not verified against Hansen's paper). The last removal's area is 8·10⁻²¹ per the 2015 correction.

events.what_happened: Peter Brass and Mehrbod Sharifi, 'A lower bound for Lebesgue's universal cover problem', Int. J. Computational Geometry & Applications 15(5) (2005), 537-544, doi 10.1142/S0218195905001828. Uses a disc, an equilateral triangle and a regular pentagon of diameter one as test sets; a subdivision over the five-parameter family of placements gives every convex universal cover area ≥ 0.832.
events.delivers: Lower bound 0.832 (0.83222 as quoted in Chen's 2026 note) on the minimum convex cover area, within the three-test-set framework.
events.remains: Exact value and minimising shape; the gap to the upper bound 0.84409.

checked_by.who: International Journal of Computational Geometry & Applications (refereed journal) and its referees
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 2005; Mishra's 2026 paper says the bound 'has stood since 2005 and is still the best that has been refereed'
checked_by.where: https://doi.org/10.1142/S0218195905001828 (DOI from a search result; not opened)

events.direction: Lower bound: raises the floor on the minimum to 0.832; does not identify the minimiser.

events.what_happened: Philip Gibbs, 'A New Slant on Lebesgue's Universal Covering Problem', arXiv:1401.8217 (v1 29 Jan 2014; v2 19 Feb 2014). A computational study that leads to conjectures; gives an upper bound 0.844113 by removing corners from a regular hexagon tilted at a small angle; proposes curves of constant width as test sets; simulations suggest the minimum is near 0.84408.
events.delivers: Upper bound 0.844113 for the minimum convex cover area, which the abstract says is proved independently of its conjectures. The 0.84408 minimum is a simulation-based estimate, not a bound.
events.directly_checkable: The corner-removal construction is explicit; the PDF could not be read here, so the coordinates were not checked.
events.direction: Upper bound: cuts the minimum downward to 0.844113; conjectures a minimum near 0.84408.
events.object: An explicit convex cover made from a regular hexagon tilted at a small angle, with corners removed; area 0.844113 (per the abstract). The boundary was not read.

events.what_happened: John Baez, Karine Bagdasaryan, Philip Gibbs, 'The Lebesgue Universal Covering Problem', arXiv:1502.01251 (v1 4 Feb 2015; v4 19 Sep 2015, comments 'numerical errors corrected'); J. Comput. Geom. 6(1) (2015) 288-299. Shows Hansen's last reduction was 8·10⁻²¹ rather than 6·10⁻¹⁸. With help from Greg Egan, finds a convex universal cover of area less than 0.8441153, lowering the previous best by 2.2·10⁻⁵.
events.revisions: v1 4 Feb 2015; v2 7 Feb 2015; v3 2 Mar 2015; v4 19 Sep 2015 ('numerical errors corrected'); journal version J. Comput. Geom. 6(1) (2015) 288-299
events.delivers: Upper bound: a convex universal cover of area less than 0.8441153. Restricted to the corner-removal family of the Pál–Sprague–Hansen shape. Also corrects the size of Hansen's last reduction.
events.remains: Exact value and minimising shape; the gap to the lower bound 0.8344.

checked_by.who: Journal of Computational Geometry (refereed journal, per DOAJ listing)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the published version; refereeing details not checked

events.directly_checkable: The covering is a finite corner-removal shape; the authors' programs (Java, Mathematica notebook) are listed in the references (not opened).
events.doubts: The arXiv comments say numerical errors were corrected in v4 (Sept 2015); the 0.8441153 figure is the final-version claim. The v1 figures were not compared.
events.direction: Upper bound: cuts the minimum downward to below 0.8441153.
events.object: An explicit convex cover obtained from the Pál–Sprague–Hansen shape by further corner removal (Gibbs's slant method); area < 0.8441153. The coordinates are in the authors' programs and Egan's Mathematica notebook, which are referenced but were not opened.

events.what_happened: Wacharin Wichiramala, 'A smaller cover for closed unit curves', arXiv:1801.08405 (v1 20 Jan 2018 only). Clips the opposite corner of the Füredi–Wetzel pentagon to get a hexagonal cover of area less than 0.11023 for closed unit curves. Not the planar diameter-one problem.
events.delivers: A cover of area < 0.11023 for closed unit curves. Different question: covers for a family of curves, not universal covers of all diameter-one sets, and not convex covers of the planar problem.
events.direction: Different question. Cuts neither way on the convex minimum.
events.object: A hexagonal cover for closed unit curves of area less than 0.11023 (abstract only).

events.what_happened: Philip Gibbs, 'An Upper Bound for Lebesgue's Covering Problem', arXiv:1810.10089 (v1 23 Oct 2018, 21 pages). Claims an upper bound of 0.8440935944 for the minimal area; refines and extends earlier covering methods. Quanta (15 Nov 2018) reports it as a paper posted online. It is the value still cited as the record in 2026 papers (Mishra, Chen) and on Wikipedia.
events.delivers: Upper bound 0.8440935944 for the minimal convex cover area. The minimising shape is not identified in the abstract read.
events.remains: Exact value and minimising shape; the lower-bound gap to 0.8344.
events.directly_checkable: The construction is explicit (refinement of the BBG 2015 family), but the PDF could not be read here.
events.direction: Upper bound: cuts the minimum downward to 0.8440935944.
events.object: An explicit convex cover refining the BBG 2015 corner-removal construction, with area 0.8440935944 (per Mishra's and Chen's descriptions and the abstract). Its boundary was not read.

events.what_happened: Mook Kwon Jung, Sang Duk Yoon, Hee-Kap Ahn, Takeshi Tokuyama, 'Universal convex covering problems under translation and discrete rotations', arXiv:2211.14807 (27 Nov 2022). Finds the smallest convex covers for planar objects of perimeter 2 under translations and discrete rotations; an equilateral triangle of height 1 is optimal when rotation by π is allowed.
events.delivers: Smallest convex covers for a different family: planar objects of perimeter 2, under translations and discrete rotations. Different question: diameter-one sets with rotations and reflections are not treated.
events.direction: Different question (perimeter-2 objects, restricted motions). Cuts neither way on the planar minimum.
events.object: An equilateral triangle of height 1 is a convex cover for planar objects of perimeter 2 under translations plus rotation by π (abstract statement).

events.what_happened: Andrii Arman, Andriy Bondarenko, Andriy Prymak, Danylo Radchenko, 'On asymptotic Lebesgue's universal covering problem', arXiv:2512.04023 (v1 3 Dec 2025; v2 27 Sep 2026). Shows that any universal cover U in n-dimensional space has volume at least exp(−√(5/4·n log n) − O(√(n/log n)))·vol(J_n), so Jung's ball is asymptotically volume-optimal as n grows. arXiv lists the journal reference Bull. London Math. Soc. 58 (2026), no. 10, e70514.
events.revisions: v1 3 Dec 2025; v2 27 Sep 2026 (the version read); journal reference Bull. London Math. Soc. 58 (2026), e70514
events.delivers: A high-dimensional asymptotic volume lower bound for universal covers in n dimensions, as n tends to infinity, relative to Jung's ball. Different question: the planar problem appears only as motivation.

checked_by.who: Bull. London Math. Soc. (journal of record, per arXiv journal reference); the paper acknowledges a referee
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (2026); the acknowledgements thank a referee and Gil Kalai's blog comments

events.direction: Different question (n-dimensional volume as n tends to infinity). Cuts neither way on the planar minimum.
events.object: No new covering set: a volume lower bound for all n-dimensional universal covers, showing Jung's ball J_n (radius √(n/(2n+2))) is asymptotically volume-optimal. Non-constructive for the lower bound.

events.what_happened: Arno Pauly, talk 'Computability of the Lebesgue Universal Covering problem', Theory Lab, Computational Foundry, Swansea University, 27 Feb 2025 (seminar listing). The listing says the minimal area of a convex planar universal cover is a computable real, with a concrete algorithm that is not practical. No paper or preprint was found; the listing names no coauthors and gives no link. Dated to the talk because no written argument was located.
events.delivers: A qualitative property of the minimum: its value is computable, by a stated algorithm. No numerical bound and no minimising shape, as far as the listing says. Different question from the value itself: computability, not the number.
events.remains: The value and the minimising shape (parts (1) and (2) of problem_asks).
events.direction: Computability of the same constant. Cuts toward nothing numerically.

events.what_happened: Yizhen Chen, 'Note on Lebesgue's universal cover problem', arXiv:2607.27227 (v1 11 Jul 2026; v2 6 Aug 2026). The results are in R³ and R^d: the minimum volume of a convex universal cover in R³ lies in (0.545193, 0.655984); a regular dodecahedron circumscribing the unit-diameter ball is not a universal cover (answering Chakerian); there is an infinite family of centrally symmetric polytopes in R^d with d(d+1) facets that are universal covers, proving Makeev's conjecture for the maximum count. The same 3D volume bounds were announced in a Stanford talk on 10 June 2025; the arXiv write-up is used as the date. The planar problem appears only as context.
events.revisions: v1 11 Jul 2026; v2 6 Aug 2026 (the version read)
events.delivers: Different question: R³ volume bounds (0.545193 to 0.655984), a dodecahedron non-universality result in R³, and facet-count results in R^d. No planar result. The planar range it quotes, (0.83222, 0.8440936), is the existing record, not a new bound.
events.remains: All of problem_asks for the plane.
events.directly_checkable: The dodecahedron non-universality claim is a finite geometric check, not performed here.
events.direction: Different question (3D and higher-dimensional). Cuts neither way on the planar minimum.
events.object: A regular dodecahedron circumscribing the unit-diameter ball is shown not to be a universal cover in R³, and an infinite family of centrally symmetric polytopes in R^d with d(d+1) facets is shown to be universal covers. These are 3D and d-dimensional objects, not planar.

events.what_happened: Niantao Xie, 'A Certified Lower Bound for Lebesgue's Universal Cover Problem', arXiv:2606.04458 (v1 3 Jun 2026; v2 4 Jun; v3 13 Jun; v4 8 Jul 2026). Proves α_cvx ≥ 0.833, the infimum of areas of convex universal covers, within the Brass–Sharifi three-test-set framework (disc, equilateral triangle, regular pentagon of diameter one). Uses a finite cover of the parameter domain with local certificates, an inner-witness polygon, and outward-rounded interval arithmetic (Moore). Certificate and verification code are in a linked GitHub repository.
events.revisions: v1 3 Jun 2026; v2 4 Jun 2026; v3 13 Jun 2026; v4 8 Jul 2026 (current)
events.delivers: Lower bound 0.833 on the minimum area of any convex universal cover, within the Brass–Sharifi three-test-set framework. No upper bound.
events.remains: Exact value and minimising shape; the gap to the upper bound 0.84409.

machine_checked.system: Author's deterministic Python verifier and certificate records (the README describes a verifier, not a proof assistant)

events.directly_checkable: The finite certificate and verifier are in the linked repository (the owner account is not verified as the author's). Not run here.
events.direction: Lower bound: raises the floor from 0.832 to 0.833. Cuts up on the minimum.
events.object: No covering set (this is a lower bound). The object is a finite certificate: finitely many parameter domains with local lower-bound certificates and inner-witness polygons whose areas are bounded below with interval estimates. The data are in the repository and were not read in full.

events.what_happened: Shuai Zeng, 'An exact hierarchy for Lebesgue's universal covering constant and a certified 0.834 lower bound', arXiv:2609.01284 (v1 1 Sep 2026 only). Introduces a Reuleaux-type variational hierarchy of finite-arc values Λ_M with a_Leb = lim Λ_M and 0 ≤ a_Leb − Λ_M ≤ C·M⁻². An outward-rounded interval certificate for a regular finite Reuleaux subtest proves a_Leb ≥ 0.834. Improves the Brass–Sharifi 2005 benchmark.
events.delivers: Lower bound 0.834 on the convex universal-cover constant (certified by one finite Reuleaux subtest). Also identifies the constant as the limit of a sequence of lower-bound values with an explicit O(M⁻²) error rate. No upper bound.
events.remains: Exact value and minimising shape; the gap to the upper bound 0.84409.

machine_checked.system: Author's standalone Python verifier with outward-rounded interval arithmetic (name not given in the text read)

events.directly_checkable: The certificate data and standalone verifier are in an archived repository, cited as reference 19, whose location was not identified. No Zenodo record found.
events.direction: Lower bound: raises the floor to 0.834, and gives a convergent lower-bound hierarchy for the constant. Cuts up on the minimum.
events.object: No covering set. The object is a finite Reuleaux-type subtest with an outward-rounded interval certificate showing a_Leb ≥ 0.834.

events.what_happened: Ujjwal Mishra (single author; no affiliation on the arXiv page), 'Curves of constant width and Lebesgue's covering problem', arXiv:2608.30538 (v1 31 Aug 2026; v2 1 Sep 2026; cs.CG, math.MG). Proves that every convex universal cover has area at least 0.8344. Uses curves of constant width as test sets (disc, Reuleaux triangle, Reuleaux pentagon), an analytic reduction, and an exhaustive branch-and-bound subdivision of the five-dimensional placement space, recorded as a certificate of 486,799,600 nodes and checked by the author's own independent verifier. The code and certificates are in a public GitHub repository whose README gives the expected output 'VERIFIED: a >= 0.8344'. The paper says 0.832 'is still the best that has been refereed'.
events.revisions: v1 31 Aug 2026; v2 1 Sep 2026 (the version read)
events.delivers: Lower bound 0.8344 on the minimum area of any convex universal cover of planar diameter-one sets. The upper bound is not changed; the paper cites 0.8440935944 (Gibbs 2018) as the current record. The paper says the three-set family cannot pass about 0.8336, which is why a new test family was used.
events.remains: The exact value and the minimising shape; the gap 0.8344 to 0.84409.

machine_checked.system: Author's own branch-and-bound certificate generator and independent verifier (verifyB.py), in Python; not a proof assistant

events.directly_checkable: The README gives a quick check (minutes, on a small control certificate) and a full check (about 15 hours on eight cores) on the headline certificate, with a SHA-256 manifest. Not run here.
events.doubts: The certificate evaluates convex-hull areas in floating point, with a rigorous floating-point error bound of 1.72e-9 against a worst leaf slack of 1.24e-5 (README). The paper says it does not use interval arithmetic. No specific error is identified. This is a method point for the later pass, not a reported error.
events.direction: Lower bound: raises the floor from 0.833 to 0.8344. Cuts up on the minimum.
events.object: No covering set (this is a lower bound). The object is a finite certificate: 486,799,600 nodes of a branch-and-bound over the five-dimensional placement space of three constant-width test sets (disc, Reuleaux triangle, Reuleaux pentagon). Each leaf bounds the convex-hull area of the placed sets from below.

ai.disclosed_cost: No AI compute disclosed. Non-AI compute from the repository README: certificate generation took 591.1 minutes; full verification about 15 hours on eight cores.

disputes.summary: Hansen (1992) stated his last corner removal as 6·10⁻¹⁸ in area; Baez, Bagdasaryan and Gibbs (2015) show it is 8·10⁻²¹. This corrects the size of the claimed reduction; it does not dispute the existence of the cover.

summary: Across 35 web searches and the page reads listed below, I found no event since 26 January 2024 that settles the problem, no change to the upper bound, and no AI system credited with any of the mathematics. Three post-2024 events move the lower bound on the minimum convex-cover area: Xie (arXiv 2606.04458, 3 June 2026) certifies 0.833 within the Brass–Sharifi three-test-set framework; Mishra (arXiv 2608.30538, 31 August 2026) certifies 0.8344 with constant-width test sets and a 486,799,600-node branch-and-bound certificate, checked by the author's own verifier in a public repository; Zeng (arXiv 2609.01284, 1 September 2026) certifies 0.834 with a Reuleaux subtest and also proves the constant is the limit of a lower-bound hierarchy with an O(M⁻²) error rate. Mishra's bound is the strongest. Zeng's came a day later and is weaker, and neither paper cites the other in the text I could read. None of the three is reported as refereed; Mishra says the 0.832 bound 'is still the best that has been refereed'. The upper bound is still Gibbs's 0.8440935944, a 2018 preprint whose PDF I could not read; I found no expert verification of it, though the 2026 papers and Wikipedia treat it as the record. Pre-window history is recorded: Pál 1920, Sprague 1936, Duff 1980 (non-convex, a different question), Hansen 1992 (with the 2015 correction), Brass–Sharifi 2005, Gibbs 2014, Baez–Bagdasaryan–Gibbs 2015, Wichiramala 2018 (closed curves, different question) and Jung et al. 2022 (perimeter-2 variant, different question). Two 2025–26 items concern other questions: Arman et al. (high-dimensional volume, journal version Bull. LMS 2026) and Chen (R³ volume and dodecahedron/facet results; the planar range it quotes is the existing record). Pauly's talk (27 February 2025) claims the minimal area is a computable real; I found no paper, so that rests on a seminar listing. Close calls: (i) whether a lower-bound move counts as moving a quantity the problem names. The problem asks for the minimum area and its shape, so these bounds move a named quantity but settle neither part; I recorded them as moves, not resolutions. (ii) Xie's acknowledgement says 'software-assisted editorial tools for copyediting'. It names no system and does not say AI, so I set none_found true and flag it here. (iii) Zeng's acknowledgement says 'Large language models were used for language editing, formatting assistance, and consistency checks', with the author reviewing all outputs. No model is named and the use is peripheral, so ai.systems is empty and none_found is false. AI search: no source credits an AI system with the mathematics. The full texts of Mishra, Chen, Arman et al. and Xie contain no AI statement beyond the Xie copyediting line. The computing that is disclosed (exhaustive branch-and-bound, interval and floating-point certificates, Mathematica and Java programs, Gibbs's numerical simulations) is not AI. The only AI-related hits were OpenAI's May 2026 Erdős unit-distance announcement and Epoch's Erdős benchmark, which do not mention this problem. Wikipedia's cached copy has a last-edit date of 25 February 2023 and predates all the 2026 developments.
competing_reading: Read narrowly, none of the 2026 lower bounds moves the problem, since each bounds a named quantity without resolving the value or identifying the shape. Under a settled-or-not rule the record stays open, and none of the post-2024 events would count. Read broadly, Mishra's 0.8344 and Zeng's convergent hierarchy are the most substantial post-2024 progress on the value, and Pauly's computability claim is a second, qualitative event that would count only if its paper appears. On AI, Xie's 'software-assisted editorial tools for copyediting' could be read as an AI tool, but the source does not say so. Zeng's sentence mentions 'consistency checks' as well as editing, which a reader could weigh as more than editing; the authors describe the outputs as reviewed and do not credit them with any mathematics.
what_would_settle_it: For the lower bounds: a run of the headline verifiers (Mishra's verifyB.py on the 0.8344 certificate; Xie's and Zeng's verification commands) by someone other than the authors, and any refereed publication. For the upper bound: the full text of Gibbs 2018 (not readable here) and an independent check of its construction, plus any new covering below 0.8440935944. For Pauly: the paper itself, if it exists, and whether its algorithm yields a numerical value. For AI: the tools named in Xie's acknowledgement, and any lab announcement or paper naming a system on this problem.
